items.meaning: To start the meeting or discussion.
items.example: Right, everyone's here, so let's kick off this morning's session.
items.plain: Right, everyone's here, so let's start this morning's session.
items.note: Informal but common way to begin a meeting. Used by the chair.

items.meaning: To quickly review the list of topics for discussion.
items.example: Before we dive in, let's quickly run through the agenda for today.
items.plain: Before we dive in, let's quickly review the topics for today.
items.note: Standard phrase for outlining meeting topics. Neutral tone.

items.meaning: To start a process or activity.
items.example: We need to make a decision today to really get the ball rolling on this project.
items.plain: We need to make a decision today to really start this project.
items.note: Common idiom for initiating something. Can be used by anyone.

items.meaning: To briefly connect with someone to discuss something.
items.example: Let's touch base next week to see how the implementation is progressing.
items.plain: Let's talk next week to see how the implementation is progressing.
items.note: Informal but widely used in professional settings.

items.meaning: To return to a previous topic later in the discussion.
items.example: That's a good point, but let's circle back to it after we've covered the main items.
items.plain: That's a good point, but let's return to it after we've covered the main items.
items.note: Useful for managing tangents and keeping discussions on track.

items.meaning: To suggest a plan or idea for consideration.
items.example: I'd like to put forward a proposal for restructuring the team.
items.plain: I'd like to suggest a plan for restructuring the team.
items.note: Formal way to introduce an idea for discussion.

items.meaning: To express a worry or doubt about something.
items.example: I need to raise a concern about the proposed timeline for delivery.
items.plain: I need to express a worry about the proposed timeline for delivery.
items.note: Polite and professional way to voice an objection or worry.

items.meaning: To listen to someone completely before responding.
items.example: Just hear me out for a moment before you jump to conclusions about the budget.
items.plain: Just listen to me for a moment before you jump to conclusions about the budget.
items.note: Used when you anticipate interruption or disagreement. Slightly informal.

items.meaning: To consider a situation from a broader perspective.
items.example: Before we get into the details, let's take a step back and look at the overall strategy.
items.plain: Before we get into the details, let's consider the overall strategy.
items.note: Encourages a broader view. Can be used by anyone.

items.meaning: To have a shared understanding or agreement.
items.example: I just want to make sure we're all on the same page regarding the project goals.
items.plain: I just want to make sure we all understand the project goals in the same way.
items.note: Common idiom for confirming mutual understanding.

items.meaning: To clarify the main point you are trying to make.
items.example: What I'm getting at is, we need to prioritize efficiency over new features right now.
items.plain: My main point is, we need to prioritize efficiency over new features right now.
items.note: Useful for rephrasing or emphasizing your core message.

items.meaning: To introduce your personal opinion or perspective.
items.example: The way I see it, we have two viable options for moving forward.
items.plain: In my opinion, we have two viable options for moving forward.
items.note: A common and polite way to offer your viewpoint.

items.meaning: To clarify a misunderstanding or nuance your point.
items.example: It's not so much that I disagree, but rather I have some reservations about the timing.
items.plain: I don't exactly disagree, but I have some reservations about the timing.
items.note: Helps to explain what you don't mean before stating what you do mean.

items.meaning: To promise to speak concisely.
items.example: I know we're short on time, so I'll keep it brief.
items.plain: I know we're short on time, so I'll speak briefly.
items.note: Polite way to signal you won't take up much time.

items.meaning: To ask for or provide more precise information.
items.example: Just to clarify, are we talking about the Q3 or Q4 budget projections?
items.plain: Can you clarify, are we talking about the Q3 or Q4 budget projections?
items.note: Common phrase for seeking or offering clarification.

items.meaning: To encourage progress or speed up a discussion.
items.example: We're running out of time, so let's try to move things along.
items.plain: We're running out of time, so let's try to speed up.
items.note: Used by the chair or someone trying to manage time.

items.meaning: To discuss a specific topic outside of the current meeting.
items.example: That's a detailed point, perhaps we should take that offline with the relevant team.
items.plain: That's a detailed point, perhaps we should discuss that separately with the relevant team.
items.note: Professional way to defer a discussion that is too specific or lengthy for the current meeting.

items.meaning: A list of topics to be discussed later, not in the current meeting.
items.example: Let's put that idea in the parking lot for a future discussion.
items.plain: Let's save that idea for a future discussion.
items.note: Common business jargon for deferring topics.

items.meaning: To examine something in more detail.
items.example: We need to drill down into the sales figures to understand the dip.
items.plain: We need to examine the sales figures in more detail to understand the dip.
items.note: Implies a thorough, in-depth investigation.

items.meaning: To provide information that makes something clearer.
items.example: Can anyone shed some light on why the project was delayed?
items.plain: Can anyone explain why the project was delayed?
items.note: Asks for an explanation or clarification.

items.meaning: To ask someone to be patient while you do something.
items.example: Please bear with me for a moment while I pull up the relevant data.
items.plain: Please be patient for a moment while I pull up the relevant data.
items.note: Polite request for patience, often when there's a slight delay.

items.meaning: To get straight to the main point without unnecessary details.
items.example: Let's cut to the chase; what's the bottom line on this budget proposal?
items.plain: Let's get to the main point; what's the bottom line on this budget proposal?
items.note: Informal but common, used when time is short or patience is thin.

items.meaning: To summarize a lengthy explanation concisely.
items.example: Long story short, the client decided to go with a different vendor.
items.plain: In summary, the client decided to go with a different vendor.
items.note: Very informal, but often used in professional settings to quickly summarize.

items.meaning: To state the most important fact or consequence.
items.example: The bottom line is, we need to increase our market share to remain competitive.
items.plain: The most important fact is, we need to increase our market share to remain competitive.
items.note: Emphasizes the crucial point or outcome.

items.meaning: To accept responsibility for a task or outcome.
items.example: Who will take ownership of coordinating the next steps for this initiative?
items.plain: Who will be responsible for coordinating the next steps for this initiative?
items.note: Professional way to assign responsibility.

items.meaning: To check the progress of something or take further action.
items.example: I'll follow up on those action items by the end of the week.
items.plain: I'll check the progress of those action items by the end of the week.
items.note: Standard phrase for checking status or continuing a task.

items.meaning: To include someone in a discussion or communication.
items.example: Please loop me in on any developments regarding the new software rollout.
items.plain: Please include me in any developments regarding the new software rollout.
items.note: Informal but very common in business.

items.meaning: To contribute something valuable to a discussion or project.
items.example: What unique skills or perspectives can you bring to the table for this task force?
items.plain: What unique skills or perspectives can you contribute to this task force?
items.note: Refers to contributions, often skills or ideas.

items.meaning: To invite others to speak or ask questions.
items.example: I'd like to open the floor for any questions or comments on the presentation.
items.plain: I'd like to invite questions or comments on the presentation.
items.note: Formal phrase used by a chair to invite participation.

items.meaning: To pause briefly to consider something.
items.example: Let's take a moment to review the key takeaways from our discussion.
items.plain: Let's pause briefly to review the key takeaways from our discussion.
items.note: Suggests a short pause for reflection or review.

items.meaning: To briefly summarize the main points discussed.
items.example: Just to recap, we've agreed on the budget and the project lead.
items.plain: To summarize, we've agreed on the budget and the project lead.
items.note: Common way to summarize before moving on or concluding.

items.meaning: To provide a brief summary of the main points.
items.example: To sum up, we need to finalize the proposal by Friday.
items.plain: To summarize, we need to finalize the proposal by Friday.
items.note: Standard phrase for summarizing.

items.meaning: The most important piece of information or conclusion.
items.example: The key takeaway from this meeting is our new marketing strategy.
items.plain: The most important conclusion from this meeting is our new marketing strategy.
items.note: Refers to the main point to remember.

items.meaning: A specific task assigned to someone to be completed.
items.example: Let's list the action items and assign owners before we close.
items.plain: Let's list the tasks and assign owners before we close.
items.note: Standard business term for a task resulting from a meeting.

items.meaning: From this point onwards; in the future.
items.example: Moving forward, all communication will go through the project manager.
items.plain: From now on, all communication will go through the project manager.
items.note: Common discourse marker for indicating future plans.

items.meaning: From this point onwards; in the future.
items.example: Going forward, we'll schedule these check-ins bi-weekly.
items.plain: From now on, we'll schedule these check-ins bi-weekly.
items.note: Interchangeable with "moving forward."

items.meaning: Available for discussion or consideration.
items.example: We have several options on the table for the new office location.
items.plain: We have several options available for the new office location.
items.note: Refers to ideas or proposals currently being considered.

items.meaning: To understand and accept an idea or suggestion.
items.example: I'll take that on board and incorporate it into the revised plan.
items.plain: I'll consider that and incorporate it into the revised plan.
items.note: British English, means to consider and accept advice or information.

items.meaning: To temporarily set aside a topic for later discussion.
items.example: That's an interesting point, but let's put a pin in it for now and return later.
items.plain: That's an interesting point, but let's save it for now and return later.
items.note: Informal, but common in business to defer a topic.

items.meaning: To ensure there is no misunderstanding.
items.example: Just to be clear, we're aiming for a soft launch next month, not a full release.
items.plain: To ensure no misunderstanding, we're aiming for a soft launch next month, not a full release.
items.note: Used to emphasize or rephrase for clarity.

items.meaning: To politely interrupt a speaker.
items.example: I'd like to interject here with a quick question about the data.
items.plain: I'd like to interrupt here with a quick question about the data.
items.note: Formal and polite way to interrupt.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask for permission to speak or interrupt.
items.example: If I may, I think we're overlooking a crucial aspect of the budget.
items.plain: May I speak? I think we're overlooking a crucial aspect of the budget.
items.note: Very polite, often used to soften an interruption or strong opinion.

items.meaning: To politely express disagreement, often before a critical comment.
items.example: With all due respect, I don't think that approach will yield the desired results.
items.plain: I respectfully disagree, I don't think that approach will yield the desired results.
items.note: Formal and often signals a strong, but polite, disagreement.

items.meaning: A request for more specific information.
items.example: I have a point of clarification regarding the project scope.
items.plain: I have a question asking for more specific information regarding the project scope.
items.note: Formal way to ask for clarification.

items.meaning: To postpone a discussion until a later time.
items.example: Given the time, I suggest we table a discussion until our next meeting.
items.plain: Given the time, I suggest we postpone this discussion until our next meeting.
items.note: In American English, this means to postpone. In British English, it means to propose for discussion.

items.meaning: To deviate from the main topic of discussion.
items.example: Let's try not to get sidetracked by minor details; we have a lot to cover.
items.plain: Let's try not to deviate from the main topic by minor details; we have a lot to cover.
items.note: Used to keep a discussion focused.

items.meaning: To remain focused on the main topic or goal.
items.example: We need to stay on track to ensure we cover all agenda items.
items.plain: We need to remain focused to ensure we cover all agenda items.
items.note: Encourages focus and adherence to the agenda.

items.meaning: To redirect the discussion to the main topic.
items.example: If I could just bring us back to the budget discussion for a moment.
items.plain: If I could just redirect us to the budget discussion for a moment.
items.note: Polite way to steer a conversation back to the agenda.

items.meaning: To argue against a popular idea to test its validity.
items.example: Just to play devil's advocate, what if the market doesn't respond as we expect?
items.plain: To challenge the idea, what if the market doesn't respond as we expect?
items.note: Used to introduce a counter-argument or challenge a consensus.

items.meaning: To introduce your personal viewpoint or opinion.
items.example: From my perspective, the biggest challenge is resource allocation.
items.plain: In my opinion, the biggest challenge is resource allocation.
items.note: A polite and common way to share your view.

items.meaning: To contribute an additional point to the discussion.
items.example: I'd like to add that our previous attempts faced similar hurdles.
items.plain: I'd like to also say that our previous attempts faced similar hurdles.
items.note: Simple and direct way to contribute.

items.meaning: To express strong agreement with someone.
items.example: I couldn't agree more with your assessment of the market trends.
items.plain: I completely agree with your assessment of the market trends.
items.note: Strong expression of agreement.

items.meaning: To politely express disagreement.
items.example: I beg to differ on that point; our data suggests a different outcome.
items.plain: I respectfully disagree on that point; our data suggests a different outcome.
items.note: Formal and polite way to disagree.

items.meaning: To postpone a discussion until a later time.
items.example: That's a complex issue, so let's table that for a dedicated session.
items.plain: That's a complex issue, so let's postpone that for a dedicated session.
items.note: American English meaning: to postpone. Be aware of British English difference.

items.meaning: To write down important information during a meeting.
items.example: Could someone please take notes for the meeting minutes?
items.plain: Could someone please write down important information for the meeting minutes?
items.note: Standard phrase for recording information.

items.meaning: The official written record of what was discussed and decided.
items.example: Please circulate the minutes of the meeting by tomorrow morning.
items.plain: Please circulate the official written record of what was discussed by tomorrow morning.
items.note: Formal term for the official record of a meeting.

items.meaning: To formally end a meeting.
items.example: I propose we adjourn the meeting and reconvene next week.
items.plain: I propose we formally end the meeting and reconvene next week.
items.note: Formal way to end a meeting.

items.meaning: To conclude a discussion or meeting.
items.example: We're almost out of time, so let's start to wrap things up.
items.plain: We're almost out of time, so let's start to conclude.
items.note: Informal but very common way to signal the end of a meeting.

items.meaning: To have no more time available.
items.example: We're going to run out of time if we don't stick to the agenda.
items.plain: We won't have enough time if we don't stick to the agenda.
items.note: Common phrase for time management.

items.meaning: To distribute available assets or personnel for tasks.
items.example: We need to carefully allocate resources for the upcoming project phases.
items.plain: We need to carefully distribute assets for the upcoming project phases.
items.note: Standard business term for managing assets.

items.meaning: To establish clear standards or anticipated outcomes.
items.example: It's important to set expectations with the client from the outset.
items.plain: It's important to establish clear anticipated outcomes with the client from the outset.
items.note: Crucial for managing projects and relationships.

items.meaning: To guide what others anticipate, often to prevent disappointment.
items.example: We need to manage expectations regarding the project's delivery date.
items.plain: We need to guide what others anticipate regarding the project's delivery date.
items.note: Often used when there's a risk of over-promising or under-delivering.

items.meaning: To gain agreement or support from others.
items.example: We need to present a strong case to get buy-in from senior management.
items.plain: We need to present a strong case to gain agreement from senior management.
items.note: Informal but widely used in business for gaining approval.

items.meaning: To resist or object to a proposal or decision.
items.example: I might have to push back on that deadline; it seems unrealistic.
items.plain: I might have to object to that deadline; it seems unrealistic.
items.note: Informal but common for expressing resistance.

items.meaning: To formally ask for a decision by counting opinions.
items.example: If there are no further objections, let's take a vote on the proposal.
items.plain: If there are no further objections, let's formally decide on the proposal.
items.note: Standard procedure for making a collective decision.

items.meaning: A decision reached by general agreement among all members.
items.example: We aim for a consensus decision on all major strategic points.
items.plain: We aim for a decision reached by general agreement on all major strategic points.
items.note: Emphasizes agreement rather than simple majority.

items.meaning: Available for people to talk about and give opinions on.
items.example: This topic is now open for discussion, please share your thoughts.
items.plain: This topic is now available for people to talk about, please share your thoughts.
items.note: Used by the chair to invite input.

items.meaning: To rephrase something for clarity or emphasis.
items.example: To put it another way, our current approach isn't sustainable long-term.
items.plain: To rephrase, our current approach isn't sustainable long-term.
items.note: Useful for clarifying a point or offering a different perspective.

items.meaning: To repeat a point for emphasis or clarity.
items.example: Just to reiterate, the deadline for submissions is Friday at 5 PM.
items.plain: To repeat, the deadline for submissions is Friday at 5 PM.
items.note: Used to emphasize an important piece of information.

items.meaning: To formally suggest an idea or plan.
items.example: I'd like to propose that we form a small working group for this task.
items.plain: I'd like to suggest that we form a small working group for this task.
items.note: Formal and polite way to make a suggestion.

items.meaning: To introduce your personal viewpoint or position.
items.example: From my standpoint, the risks outweigh the potential benefits at this stage.
items.plain: In my opinion, the risks outweigh the potential benefits at this stage.
items.note: Similar to "from my perspective," slightly more formal.

items.meaning: To proceed to the next topic on the agenda.
items.example: We've spent enough time on this, so let's move on to the next item.
items.plain: We've spent enough time on this, so let's proceed to the next item.
items.note: Used by the chair to transition between topics.

items.meaning: To politely indicate that you don't understand.
items.example: I'm afraid I don't follow your logic regarding the budget cuts.
items.plain: I don't understand your logic regarding the budget cuts.
items.note: Polite and indirect way to express confusion.

items.meaning: To ask for more details or a fuller explanation.
items.example: Could you elaborate on the potential impact of these changes?
items.plain: Could you give more details on the potential impact of these changes?
items.note: Polite way to ask for more information.

items.meaning: To verify information or understanding.
items.example: Just to confirm, we're meeting at 10 AM on Tuesday, correct?
items.plain: To verify, we're meeting at 10 AM on Tuesday, correct?
items.note: Used to double-check details.

items.meaning: To politely add your opinion or comment to a discussion.
items.example: I'd like to chime in here with a thought on the marketing strategy.
items.plain: I'd like to add my opinion here with a thought on the marketing strategy.
items.note: Informal but common way to contribute to a conversation.

items.meaning: To begin the meeting or activity.
items.example: Good morning everyone, let's get started with today's agenda.
items.plain: Good morning everyone, let's begin with today's agenda.
items.note: Common and straightforward way to open a meeting.

items.meaning: Before ending the meeting.
items.example: Before we conclude, are there any final questions or points?
items.plain: Before we end the meeting, are there any final questions or points?
items.note: Standard phrase for inviting last-minute input.

items.meaning: To begin the meeting or a specific topic immediately.
items.example: Alright team, we have a lot to cover today, so let's dive in.
items.plain: We have a lot to cover, so let's start now.
items.note: Informal but common way to start a meeting or a new topic.

items.meaning: To start focusing on the main, serious topics of the meeting.
items.example: Now that everyone's here, let's get down to business and discuss the Q3 results.
items.plain: Everyone is here, so let's start discussing the Q3 results.
items.note: Signals a shift from informal chat to serious work.

items.meaning: To discuss the most important aspects of a topic.
items.example: Before we go into detail, let's quickly cover the main points of the project update.
items.plain: Let's quickly discuss the most important aspects of the project update.
items.note: Useful for structuring a discussion or presentation.

items.meaning: To remain focused on the planned topics for the meeting.
items.example: I know there are other issues, but for now, let's try to stick to the agenda.
items.plain: Let's try to remain focused on the planned topics for this meeting.
items.note: A polite way to redirect a discussion that is going off-topic.

items.meaning: To exceed the scheduled duration of the meeting.
items.example: We're starting to run over time, so let's try to keep our comments concise.
items.plain: We are exceeding the scheduled duration, so let's be concise.
items.note: Often used as a gentle warning to speed up.

items.meaning: To assign a specific period for discussing a particular item.
items.example: We should allocate time for a Q&A session at the end of the presentation.
items.plain: We should assign a specific period for a Q&A session.
items.note: Used when planning or managing the meeting schedule.

items.meaning: To deal with or respond to a specific issue or comment.
items.example: Before we move on, I'd like to address a point Sarah raised earlier.
items.plain: Before we move on, I want to respond to Sarah's earlier comment.
items.note: Common in formal and semi-formal discussions.

items.meaning: To ask someone a question directly.
items.example: I'd like to put a question to the finance team regarding these figures.
items.plain: I want to ask the finance team a question about these figures.
items.note: Slightly more formal than "ask a question".

items.meaning: To return to a topic or issue later in the discussion.
items.example: That's an interesting thought, but let's come back to it after we've covered the main agenda.
items.plain: That's interesting, but let's discuss it later after the main agenda.
items.note: Similar to "circle back to" but perhaps slightly less formal.

items.meaning: To write down something important to remember or act upon.
items.example: Could someone please take a note of that action item for the minutes?
items.plain: Could someone please write down that action item for the minutes?
items.note: Used for recording specific details or tasks.

items.meaning: To ask someone for their opinion or perspective on a topic.
items.example: Before we decide, I'd like to get your thoughts on the proposed marketing strategy.
items.plain: Before we decide, I'd like to hear your opinion on the marketing strategy.
items.note: A polite way to invite participation and gather input.

items.meaning: To ask for someone's opinion or reaction to something.
items.example: We've discussed the options, now what are your thoughts on the best way forward?
items.plain: We've discussed the options, now what do you think is the best way forward?
items.note: A direct but open-ended question to encourage discussion.

items.meaning: To introduce a comment or contribution, often to soften it.
items.example: I just wanted to say that I think we're overlooking a key risk here.
items.plain: I think we're overlooking a key risk here.
items.note: A common softener when interrupting or adding a point.

items.meaning: To check one's comprehension of what has been said.
items.example: If I understand correctly, we're aiming for a launch by the end of Q2?
items.plain: Am I right that we're aiming for a launch by the end of Q2?
items.note: A polite way to seek confirmation or clarify a point.

items.meaning: To invite correction if one's understanding or statement is inaccurate.
items.example: Correct me if I'm wrong, but didn't we agree on a different approach last week?
items.plain: Didn't we agree on a different approach last week? Please tell me if I'm wrong.
items.note: A humble way to challenge or question something, inviting input.

items.meaning: To explain something in an easier, less complex way.
items.example: To put it simply, our budget won't allow for that extensive a campaign.
items.plain: Our budget won't allow for that extensive a campaign.
items.note: Used to simplify a complex idea or deliver a direct message.

items.meaning: To summarize something very briefly.
items.example: In a nutshell, we need to increase our market share by 15% next year.
items.plain: Briefly, we need to increase our market share by 15% next year.
items.note: Informal but widely used for concise summaries.

items.meaning: To quickly summarize the main points discussed so far.
items.example: To recap briefly, we've decided on the new project timeline and assigned roles.
items.plain: We've decided on the new project timeline and assigned roles.
items.note: Used to quickly remind everyone of key decisions or points.

items.meaning: To summarize the main points or decisions made.
items.example: Before we finish, let's recap the key decisions and action items.
items.plain: Before we finish, let's summarize the key decisions and action items.
items.note: A common way to conclude a section or the entire meeting.

items.meaning: To provide a brief summary of the main points.
items.example: To sum up, we need to finalize the budget by Friday and present it next week.
items.plain: We need to finalize the budget by Friday and present it next week.
items.note: A standard phrase for concluding a discussion or meeting.

items.meaning: To politely offer an idea or recommendation.
items.example: I'd like to suggest we explore alternative suppliers to reduce costs.
items.plain: I suggest we explore alternative suppliers to reduce costs.
items.note: A polite and common way to make a suggestion.

items.meaning: To propose an action or course of action to the group.
items.example: How about we take a short break before moving on to the next topic?
items.plain: Let's take a short break before moving on to the next topic.
items.note: An informal but friendly way to make a suggestion.

items.meaning: To propose a hypothetical scenario or alternative approach.
items.example: What if we shifted the launch date by a week to ensure everything is perfect?
items.plain: Should we shift the launch date by a week to ensure everything is perfect?
items.note: Used to explore possibilities or suggest a different plan.

items.meaning: To express a tendency towards a particular opinion or belief.
items.example: I'm inclined to think that the current strategy needs a significant overhaul.
items.plain: I tend to think that the current strategy needs a significant overhaul.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to express an opinion.

items.meaning: To share one's first thoughts or feelings about something.
items.example: My initial reaction is that the proposal is too ambitious for our current resources.
items.plain: My first thought is that the proposal is too ambitious for our current resources.
items.note: Useful for giving immediate, unfiltered feedback.

items.meaning: To express doubt or partial disagreement politely.
items.example: I'm not entirely convinced that this solution will address the root cause of the problem.
items.plain: I doubt this solution will address the root cause of the problem.
items.note: A soft way to express disagreement or skepticism.

items.meaning: To express doubts or concerns about a plan or idea.
items.example: I have some reservations about expanding into that market without further research.
items.plain: I have some doubts about expanding into that market without further research.
items.note: A polite and professional way to express caution or concern.

items.meaning: To acknowledge and understand someone else's argument or perspective.
items.example: I see your point about the budget constraints, but we also need to consider quality.
items.plain: I understand your argument about the budget, but we also need to consider quality.
items.note: Used to show understanding, often before presenting a counter-argument.

items.meaning: To acknowledge that someone's argument or comment is reasonable and relevant.
items.example: That's a valid point regarding the timeline; we might need to adjust it.
items.plain: Your comment about the timeline is reasonable; we might need to adjust it.
items.note: A polite way to acknowledge agreement or the strength of an argument.

items.meaning: To express full agreement with what someone has said.
items.example: I completely agree with your assessment of the market trends.
items.plain: I fully agree with your assessment of the market trends.
items.note: A strong and direct way to show agreement.

items.meaning: To formally express agreement with an opinion or decision.
items.example: After reviewing the data, I concur with the team's recommendation.
items.plain: After reviewing the data, I agree with the team's recommendation.
items.note: More formal than "I agree", often used in professional settings.

items.meaning: To indicate understanding of someone's point or argument.
items.example: I see what you mean about the potential risks, and we should address them.
items.plain: I understand your point about the potential risks, and we should address them.
items.note: A common phrase to acknowledge understanding, often before responding.

items.meaning: To politely indicate that one does not understand something.
items.example: I'm not sure I follow your logic on that last point; could you explain?
items.plain: I don't understand your logic on that last point; could you explain?
items.note: A polite way to ask for clarification.

items.meaning: To ask for a clearer explanation or more specific information.
items.example: Could you clarify what you mean by 'optimizing workflows' in this context?
items.plain: Please explain what you mean by 'optimizing workflows' in this context.
items.note: A direct and polite request for more detail or precision.

items.meaning: To provide more precise or detailed information.
items.example: To be more specific, we need to reduce costs by 10% across all departments.
items.plain: Specifically, we need to reduce costs by 10% across all departments.
items.note: Used when elaborating on a general statement.

items.meaning: To say something again in a different way to make it clearer.
items.example: Let me rephrase that: our primary goal is to enhance customer satisfaction.
items.plain: Our primary goal is to enhance customer satisfaction.
items.note: Used when you feel your previous statement wasn't clear enough.

items.meaning: To provide additional details or explanation on a topic.
items.example: To elaborate further, the market research indicates a strong demand for this feature.
items.plain: The market research indicates a strong demand for this feature.
items.note: Used to expand on a point already made.

items.meaning: To emphasize the importance of a particular point.
items.example: I'd like to underscore the urgency of completing this task by Friday.
items.plain: I want to emphasize the urgency of completing this task by Friday.
items.note: A formal way to highlight something important.

items.meaning: To introduce an important piece of information or observation.
items.example: It's worth noting that our competitors are already implementing similar strategies.
items.plain: Our competitors are already implementing similar strategies, which is important.
items.note: Used to draw attention to a relevant fact.

items.meaning: To state something officially or to ensure it is noted.
items.example: Just for the record, I did raise this concern in our previous meeting.
items.plain: I want it noted that I raised this concern in our previous meeting.
items.note: Used to ensure a point is officially acknowledged or remembered.

items.meaning: To explain something in a different, often more direct or illustrative, manner.
items.example: Let's put it this way: if we don't innovate, we'll fall behind.
items.plain: If we don't innovate, we'll fall behind.
items.note: Used to offer an alternative explanation or a more impactful statement.

items.meaning: To volunteer to be responsible for a task or action.
items.example: I'm happy to take the lead on researching potential vendors.
items.plain: I will lead the research on potential vendors.
items.note: A polite and proactive way to volunteer for a task.

items.meaning: To offer assistance with a specific task or area.
items.example: I can certainly help with drafting the initial report if needed.
items.plain: I can help draft the initial report if needed.
items.note: A polite and confident offer of support.

items.meaning: To promise to investigate or research a particular issue.
items.example: That's a good question; I'll look into that and get back to you.
items.plain: That's a good question; I will investigate it and respond to you.
items.note: A common way to take on an action item for further investigation.

items.meaning: To promise to provide an answer or information later.
items.example: I don't have that data right now, but I'll get back to you by end of day.
items.plain: I don't have that data now, but I will provide it to you by end of day.
items.note: Used when you need to find information before responding.

items.meaning: To arrange another meeting or discussion to continue a topic.
items.example: We're out of time, so let's schedule a follow-up to discuss the budget in detail.
items.plain: We're out of time, so let's arrange another meeting to discuss the budget.
items.note: A common way to ensure continuity on unresolved issues.

items.meaning: To state that a decision is required regarding a specific matter.
items.example: Before we close, we need to decide on the next steps for the project.
items.plain: Before we close, we must make a decision about the next project steps.
items.note: Used to prompt a decision from the group.

items.meaning: To ask what the general agreement or shared opinion is among the group.
items.example: We've heard all perspectives, so what's the consensus on the best approach?
items.plain: We've heard all perspectives, so what is the general agreement on the best approach?
items.note: Used to gauge the group's overall agreement.

items.meaning: To suggest a target or goal to work towards.
items.example: Let's aim for a 10% increase in sales by the end of the quarter.
items.plain: Let's target a 10% increase in sales by the end of the quarter.
items.note: Used to propose a goal or objective.

items.meaning: To formally suggest a plan or course of action.
items.example: I'd like to propose that we form a small task force to investigate this further.
items.plain: I suggest we form a small task force to investigate this further.
items.note: A formal way to make a suggestion or recommendation.

items.meaning: To indicate that one is about to speak honestly and directly.
items.example: To be frank, I don't think we have the resources for this ambitious plan.
items.plain: Honestly, I don't think we have the resources for this ambitious plan.
items.note: Used to introduce a direct or potentially critical comment.

items.meaning: To introduce one side of a two-sided argument or consideration.
items.example: On the one hand, the new system is more efficient, but on the other, it's costly.
items.plain: The new system is more efficient, but it's also costly.
items.note: Used to present contrasting points of view.

items.meaning: To introduce the contrasting side of an argument or consideration.
items.example: On the one hand, the new system is more efficient, but on the other hand, it's costly.
items.plain: The new system is more efficient, but it's also costly.
items.note: Always follows "On the one hand" to present a counterpoint.

items.meaning: To rephrase something for clarity or to summarize it differently.
items.example: The project is behind schedule; in other words, we need to accelerate our efforts.
items.plain: The project is behind schedule; we need to accelerate our efforts.
items.note: Used to simplify or clarify a previous statement.

items.meaning: To invite a specific person or group to share their thoughts.
items.example: Before we finalize, I'd like to hear from the marketing team on this.
items.plain: Before we finalize, I want the marketing team to share their thoughts.
items.note: A polite way to solicit input from specific individuals.

items.meaning: To invite general discussion or questions from the group.
items.example: We've covered the main points, so let's open it up to questions now.
items.plain: We've covered the main points, so let's take questions now.
items.note: Used to transition to a Q&A or general discussion segment.

items.meaning: To offer to respond to questions.
items.example: I'm happy to answer any questions you might have about the presentation.
items.plain: I will answer any questions you might have about the presentation.
items.note: A polite way to invite questions after a presentation or explanation.

items.meaning: To ask participants to be brief and to the point.
items.example: We have limited time, so let's keep it concise when sharing updates.
items.plain: We have limited time, so please be brief when sharing updates.
items.note: A polite reminder to be brief, often when time is short.

items.meaning: To indicate that there is not much time left in the meeting.
items.example: We're running short on time, so let's quickly decide on the next steps.
items.plain: We don't have much time left, so let's quickly decide on the next steps.
items.note: A common phrase to prompt a quick decision or wrap-up.

items.meaning: To conclude the discussion on a particular topic or the entire meeting.
items.example: We've made good progress, so let's wrap this up and move to the next item.
items.plain: We've made good progress, so let's finish this and move to the next item.
items.note: An informal but common way to signal the end of a discussion.

items.meaning: To introduce final remarks or actions before ending the meeting.
items.example: Before we close, let's confirm who is responsible for each action item.
items.plain: Before we end, let's confirm who is responsible for each action item.
items.note: A standard phrase for the final stage of a meeting.

items.meaning: To state the purpose of asking a question or rephrasing something.
items.example: To ensure clarity, could you confirm the deadline for the report?
items.plain: Could you confirm the deadline for the report so it's clear?
items.note: Used to justify a request for clarification.

items.meaning: To stress the importance of a particular point or idea.
items.example: I want to emphasize the importance of clear communication throughout this project.
items.plain: I want to stress the importance of clear communication throughout this project.
items.note: A direct way to highlight a crucial aspect.

items.meaning: To move directly to a specific topic without delay.
items.example: We have a packed agenda, so let's get straight to the budget review.
items.plain: We have a packed agenda, so let's start the budget review immediately.
items.note: Used to signal a direct approach to a topic.

items.text: I'd like to propose a motion
items.form: I'd like to propose a motion
items.meaning: To formally suggest a course of action for a vote or decision.
items.example: I'd like to propose a motion to approve the revised project plan.
items.plain: I suggest we vote to approve the revised project plan.
items.note: Very formal, typically used in structured meetings with voting procedures.

items.meaning: To formally express agreement with a proposal, allowing it to be discussed or voted on.
items.example: Sarah's idea is excellent; I second that proposal.
items.plain: Sarah's idea is excellent; I agree with that proposal.
items.note: Formal, used to support a motion or proposal.

items.text: Let's put it to a vote
items.form: Let's put it to a vote
items.meaning: To suggest that the group make a decision by voting.
items.example: We have differing opinions, so let's put it to a vote and move forward.
items.plain: We have differing opinions, so let's vote and move forward.
items.note: A common way to resolve disagreements and make a decision.

items.text: I'd like to make a point
items.form: I'd like to make a point
items.meaning: To politely introduce a comment or argument.
items.example: I'd like to make a point about the potential impact on our existing customers.
items.plain: I want to comment on the potential impact on our existing customers.
items.note: A polite way to interject or contribute to a discussion.

items.meaning: To make a very polite and tentative suggestion.
items.example: Could we perhaps consider a phased implementation instead of a full rollout?
items.plain: Should we consider a phased implementation instead of a full rollout?
items.note: A very soft and diplomatic way to suggest an alternative.

items.meaning: To politely express disagreement.
items.example: I'm afraid I disagree with the premise that this is a simple problem.
items.plain: I disagree with the idea that this is a simple problem.
items.note: A polite and common way to express disagreement.

items.meaning: To politely state that one has a different opinion or perspective.
items.example: While I understand your reasoning, I see things differently regarding the timeline.
items.plain: While I understand your reasoning, I have a different opinion regarding the timeline.
items.note: A diplomatic way to express disagreement without being confrontational.

items.meaning: To invite a specific person or group to speak.
items.example: Now, let's hear from Maria about the progress on the marketing campaign.
items.plain: Now, Maria, please tell us about the progress on the marketing campaign.
items.note: Used by the meeting chair to direct the discussion.

items.text: I'd like to hand over to
items.form: I'd like to hand over to
items.meaning: To formally transfer the speaking turn or responsibility to another person.
items.example: I'd like to hand over to John, who will present the financial projections.
items.plain: I will now let John present the financial projections.
items.note: Common when transitioning between speakers or topics.

items.meaning: To introduce the first item or speaker of the meeting.
items.example: To get us started, I'll briefly outline the objectives for today's discussion.
items.plain: I'll briefly outline the objectives for today's discussion to begin.
items.note: A common opening phrase for the meeting chair.

items.meaning: To politely suggest transitioning to the next topic on the agenda.
items.example: We've discussed this thoroughly, so shall we move on to the next agenda item?
items.plain: We've discussed this thoroughly, so let's move to the next agenda item.
items.note: A polite way to steer the meeting to the next point.

items.text: I'd like to draw your attention to
items.form: I'd like to draw your attention to
items.meaning: To direct the group's focus to a specific detail or issue.
items.example: I'd like to draw your attention to the figures on slide five, which are crucial.
items.plain: Please look at the figures on slide five, which are crucial.
items.note: A formal way to highlight important information.

items.meaning: To remind the group of an important overarching goal or principle.
items.example: While discussing details, let's not lose sight of our main objective: customer satisfaction.
items.plain: While discussing details, let's remember our main objective: customer satisfaction.
items.note: Used to keep the discussion focused on the bigger picture.

items.text: I'd like to get your input
items.form: I'd like to get your input
items.meaning: To politely ask for someone's opinion or contribution.
items.example: I'd like to get your input on the proposed changes to the project scope.
items.plain: I want your opinion on the proposed changes to the project scope.
items.note: A common and polite way to solicit feedback.

items.meaning: To ensure everyone understands what actions need to be taken after the meeting.
items.example: Before we finish, let's clarify the next steps and assign responsibilities.
items.plain: Before we finish, let's make sure everyone understands the next actions.
items.note: Essential for effective meeting outcomes.

items.meaning: To express strong belief or assurance about a future outcome or statement.
items.example: I'm confident that with this new strategy, we will achieve our targets.
items.plain: I believe strongly that with this new strategy, we will achieve our targets.
items.note: Used to convey conviction and inspire confidence.

the bottom line is.note: Checker slip: The phrase is accurately used to introduce the most important fact or main conclusion.

i'm afraid i disagree.note: Checker slip: The key accurately describes the polite disagreement expressed in the example.
